strengths: Fills a genuine gap in the DyNVS literature: existing datasets (real or physics-based) rarely combine multi-object/multi-material interaction with ground-truth 3D trajectories and physics parameters (viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, stiffness, etc.), as clearly documented in the comparison Tables 1 and 2.

Careful, material-appropriate simulation design: the authors justify the choice of solver per material (FLIP for liquids, Pyro for gas/temperature-driven buoyancy, MPM for viscoelastic, Vellum/XPBD for textiles) and document numerous scene-specific parameter tuning choices (voxel size, oversampling, sub-step count) in the appendix, indicating simulation care rather than a naive off-the-shelf pipeline.

Good breadth and diversity of scenes (17 scenes across 4 material categories, single/multi-object, 180°/360° camera coverage, monocular and multiview configurations) supporting different downstream task formulations.

Useful empirical contribution beyond just releasing data: benchmarking four recent DyNVS baselines (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM) under both monocular and multiview settings, with both quantitative (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and qualitative analysis, and a specific trajectory-level analysis (Fig. 6) showing that photorealistic RGB reconstruction does not imply physically correct point trajectories -- a genuinely useful and underappreciated finding that could redirect community focus.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility/practical usability: integration pipelines for existing SOTA models, COLMAP point clouds provided, full simulation node graphs shared for customization, and licensing of assets clearly documented (Appendix C).
weaknesses: The dataset is entirely synthetic (Houdini-rendered), and the paper only briefly acknowledges the sim-to-real gap in the limitations section without any quantitative characterization of photorealism gap or domain-transfer experiments, which limits confidence that conclusions/benchmarks will transfer to real captured video.

Scale is modest: only 17 scenes total, 4-5 per material category, which is a small benchmark for training/evaluating deep models robustly; per-scene breakdown tables show large variance, making it unclear how statistically reliable material-category-level conclusions are.

The physics ground truth (3D particle trajectories) is inherently defined on simulation particles/voxels rather than on any canonical set of visible surface points that DyNVS methods would need to predict, so it's not fully clear how outputs from Gaussian-based methods (which don't have a natural particle correspondence) are matched to ground truth for the trajectory evaluation in Fig. 6 -- the alignment/matching procedure is not described in the main text.

No new method or metric is proposed to address the identified limitation (RGB reconstruction loss not guaranteeing physical realism); the paper diagnoses a problem but leaves solving it entirely to future work, which somewhat limits the technical contribution to a benchmark/diagnostic paper.

Baseline evaluation is restricted to 4 existing GS-based DyNVS methods, none of which are physics-aware (e.g., PhysGaussian-style approaches); given the dataset's stated purpose of advancing physics-aware modeling, not including any physics-informed baseline (even from related work like PAC-NeRF or Spring-Gaus) limits the demonstrated value of the physics ground-truth annotations for actually driving physics-aware DyNVS research.

Some presentation issues: table formatting inconsistencies (e.g., bolding of best values not always consistent with reported numbers, Table 3/4), and the explanation of how subsampled particle trajectories are produced/stored (mentioned only briefly for gas) is not detailed for other materials.

Camera setups (2 or 4 cameras with spiral trajectories) are somewhat limited compared to real-world capture rigs with dozens of cameras (e.g., Neural 3D Video), which may limit the difficulty/realism of the multiview evaluation setting relative to real deployment scenarios.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing DyNVS datasets largely lack multi-body interactions and ground-truth physics information (parameters and 3D trajectories), while PhysGaia explicitly targets this by simulating four distinct material types (liquid, gas, viscoelastic, textile) with material-appropriate solvers (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, Vellum) inside a unified Houdini pipeline.

The empirical analysis (Section 5, Figures 5-6) makes a useful and well-illustrated qualitative point: current state-of-the-art Gaussian-based DyNVS methods can achieve plausible RGB reconstruction while their underlying Gaussian trajectories diverge substantially from the true physical motion, highlighting that photometric loss alone is insufficient for physical fidelity.

Reasonable engineering effort and documentation: the dataset offers both monocular and multiview configurations, multiple auxiliary modalities (depth, normal, relit images), customizable simulation node graphs, COLMAP point clouds, and integration pipelines for several baseline methods, along with a clear and compliant licensing statement for all source assets.

Comprehensive supplementary material including full per-scene quantitative breakdowns for both monocular and multiview settings and additional qualitative failure-case figures, which aids transparency and reproducibility of the baseline evaluation.
weaknesses: The paper's headline claim — that ground-truth 3D trajectories and physics parameters 'enable precise/quantitative evaluation of physical modeling' — is not actually substantiated. Section 5.2's physics-realism analysis is purely qualitative (visual trajectory comparison in Figure 6); no quantitative trajectory-based metric (e.g., endpoint error, Chamfer distance to GT particles, parameter-estimation accuracy) is reported anywhere in the main text or appendix, despite this being presented as the dataset's distinguishing advantage over prior benchmarks.

None of the four evaluated baselines (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM) are physics-integrated methods; the paper does not test any physics-aware approaches (e.g., PhysGaussian, Spring-Gaus, PhysTwin, which are discussed in related work) on PhysGaia. Since the dataset's motivation is specifically to advance physics-aware modeling, omitting any physics-informed baseline leaves the central use case of the benchmark unvalidated.

The dataset is modest in scale (17 scenes total, only 4-5 per material category) and entirely synthetic/rendered, with no real-world captures; the authors acknowledge this as a limitation but provide no analysis of sim-to-real transfer or domain gap, which limits confidence in claims about advancing 'real-world' AR/VR applications.

Per-scene physics configurations (voxel sizes, oversampling rates, sub-step counts, grid sizes) were manually tuned on a case-by-case basis with limited systematic justification, which may affect reproducibility and consistency of 'ground-truth' physical fidelity across scenes.

Claims of 'rich' and 'complex' multi-body interactions are supported only qualitatively (figures) rather than through any quantitative characterization (e.g., number/frequency of contact events, interaction complexity metrics), making it hard to assess how the interaction richness compares objectively to prior datasets beyond the coarse presence/absence table.

The paper is purely a dataset/benchmarking contribution with no proposed method or technical innovation to address the identified limitations of existing DyNVS models, somewhat limiting its technical contribution relative to a methods paper, and the diagnosis of failure causes (RGB loss insufficiency) is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated through controlled ablation.

strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap: existing DyNVS/physics-aware datasets are largely single-object/single-material, whereas PhysGaia provides genuine multi-body interactions (collisions, force exchange) across four distinct material categories (liquid, gas, viscoelastic, textile).

Rigorous, material-specific simulation methodology (FLIP for liquids, Pyro for gas, MPM for viscoelastic, Vellum/XPBD for textile) within a unified Houdini pipeline, with carefully documented per-scene physics parameters (viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, temperature) in the appendix, lending credibility to the physical accuracy claims.

Provides valuable and rarely available ground-truth signals for the field: 3D particle trajectories and physics parameters, enabling quantitative evaluation of physical reasoning/inverse estimation that RGB-only benchmarks cannot support.
Supports both monocular and multiview evaluation protocols and includes ready-to-use integration pipelines for several SOTA DyNVS baselines (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM), lowering the adoption barrier.

Thorough empirical analysis (Tables 3-4, per-scene breakdowns in appendix, multiple qualitative figures) convincingly demonstrates that current Gaussian-Splatting-based DyNVS methods achieve photorealism via local color-based fluctuation rather than physically faithful trajectories, a useful and well-supported finding that motivates the dataset's relevance.
Good documentation of licensing/provenance of assets (Table 11) and customizability via released simulation node graphs, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The dataset is purely synthetic; no real-world captures or sim-to-real validation are provided, and domain-gap mitigation is left entirely as future work (Appendix D), which limits immediate applicability to real AR/VR scenarios that the paper motivates the work with.

Modest scale (17 scenes, 4-5 per material category) — while comparable to some prior benchmarks, this is a fairly small pool for training/evaluating data-hungry deep models and for drawing strong statistical conclusions about method failure modes.

No new method or algorithmic solution is proposed; the paper is a dataset/benchmark contribution only, and the demonstrated limitations of baselines are not accompanied by any proposed mitigation or ablation pointing toward a fix.

The evaluation only includes RGB-only DyNVS baselines (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM); physics-integrated GS methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., PhysGaussian, Spring-Gaus) are not benchmarked quantitatively on PhysGaia, which would have been more informative for assessing whether physics-aware priors actually help trajectory accuracy.

The trajectory-fidelity comparison (Figure 6) is presented only qualitatively; no quantitative trajectory-error metric (e.g., Chamfer distance or endpoint error against ground-truth particle trajectories) is reported despite the dataset explicitly providing 3D trajectories for this purpose.

Camera coverage is limited (2 or 4 training cameras, two static test cameras), which may constrain the diversity of viewpoints for multiview benchmarking and could affect generalizability of the reported failure conclusions.
Minor presentation issues (occasional grammar/typos) that do not affect the core contribution but would benefit from polishing.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing DyNVS benchmarks are either photorealism-only (lacking physics ground truth) or physics-based but restricted to single objects/materials, whereas PhysGaia offers 17 scenes with rich multi-body interactions across four distinct material classes (liquid, gas, rheological substances, textile).

Provides genuinely useful ground-truth annotations (3D particle trajectories and physical parameters such as viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, temperature) that enable quantitative evaluation of physical plausibility, not just image-space photorealism, via two new metrics (Trajectory Distance and Area Under Outlier Percentages).

Careful, material-specific simulation pipeline (FLIP for liquids, Pyro for gases, MPM for rheological substances, Vellum/XPBD for textiles), with detailed physics/solver documentation in the appendix (governing equations, parameter tables, dynamic-interaction handling) that supports reproducibility and transparency.

Extensive empirical study benchmarking five recent DyNVS methods (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, MoSca, SoM) in both monocular and multiview settings, with both quantitative (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, TD/AUOP) and qualitative (trajectory visualization) analyses that convincingly reveal that current SOTA methods, despite reasonable photorealism, fail to recover physically plausible motion — a valuable and somewhat under-appreciated diagnostic finding for the field.

Good accessibility considerations: customizable source files/solvers, COLMAP point clouds, integration pipelines for several 4DGS baselines, and multiple rendered modalities (depth, normal, relighting), which should facilitate adoption by the community.
Comparative tables (Tables 1-3) against a wide range of prior DyNVS and physics-simulated datasets are thorough and clarify the paper's positioning relative to prior work.
License and provenance documentation for all 3D assets/textures is unusually complete for a benchmark paper, reducing IP concerns.
weaknesses: All scenes are purely synthetic, generated with idealized physics solvers under simplified constitutive/boundary assumptions; the paper's own limitations section concedes this, but it materially limits how well conclusions transfer to real-world capture, where sensor noise, imperfect calibration, and unmodeled material behavior dominate.

The physical-realism evaluation (TD/AUOP) is reported for only two scenes (cow, box-smoke) in the main paper, and the inverse-physics parameter estimation study uses a single scene (bouncing balls) with only two baselines — these are fairly narrow slices of the 17-scene benchmark, so the generality of the physics-realism findings is not fully substantiated by the presented evidence.

The benchmark is modest in scale (17 scenes, 4-5 per material category), which, combined with the limited camera setups (2 or 4 spiral cameras), may constrain statistical robustness and diversity of viewpoints/motions relative to what real-world capture rigs would provide.

Some evaluation metrics used to argue PhysGaia's superiority (dynamic score, FID/KID on flattened frames) are borrowed proxies not specifically validated for measuring physical complexity or realism, and their comparison to other benchmarks (Table 3, Fig. 6) mixes datasets with different content/resolution characteristics, which weakens the strength of the comparative claims.
No user study or perceptual validation is provided to corroborate that the rendered scenes are perceived as visually/physically realistic beyond FID/KID scores.

As a benchmark/analysis paper, no new method or mitigation is proposed to address the demonstrated failure modes of current DyNVS approaches; the contribution is diagnostic rather than corrective, which is appropriate for a benchmark paper but limits the immediate technical impact.

Scene generation is computationally expensive (12-24 hours for some scenes on described hardware), which could hinder easy extension of the benchmark by other researchers wanting to add new scenes/materials.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing physics-aware DyNVS benchmarks are restricted to single objects/materials (e.g., ScalarFlow, PAC-NeRF, Spring-Gaus), while PhysGaia introduces 17 scenes with rich multi-body interactions across four material categories (liquid, gas, rheological substances, textile) simulated with material-appropriate solvers (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, Vellum).

Provides comprehensive ground-truth physical information (3D particle trajectories, viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, temperature fields) that enables quantitative evaluation beyond photometric quality, which is largely absent in prior DyNVS datasets.

Introduces two new complementary metrics (Trajectory Distance and Area Under the Outlier Percentages) specifically designed to measure physical plausibility of reconstructed Gaussian trajectories rather than only RGB fidelity.

Extensive empirical study evaluates five recent DyNVS baselines (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, MoSca, SoM) under both monocular and multiview settings across all 17 scenes, and convincingly demonstrates that current methods fail to capture rich multi-body dynamics (needle-like artifacts, under-reconstruction), motivating the benchmark's necessity.

Strong supplementary documentation: detailed solver configurations, physics parameter tables, camera trajectory design, licensing information, and integration pipelines/COLMAP point clouds for reproducibility, exceeding the documentation rigor typical of benchmark papers.
Additionally demonstrates the benchmark's utility for inverse-physics parameter estimation, broadening the dataset's potential use cases beyond pure view synthesis.
weaknesses: The core physical-realism metrics (TD, AUOP) that are a headline contribution of the paper are only reported on two scenes (cow, box-smoke) out of the full 17-scene benchmark, which is a thin empirical base for validating the proposed evaluation protocol and for the claims made from it (Table 6, Figures 7-8).

The inverse-physics parameter estimation experiment (Table 7) is evaluated on only a single scene (bouncing balls) with two methods, too narrow to support general conclusions about systematic underestimation of stiffness in multi-object settings.

The entire benchmark is synthetically rendered in Houdini; while physically grounded, there is no analysis or discussion of the sim-to-real gap or how well conclusions drawn (e.g., about method failure modes) would transfer to real captured video, which is the eventual target application (AR/VR).

Photorealism comparison against existing physics datasets uses FID/KID against TinyImageNet statistics, an unconventional and somewhat indirect proxy for 'visual fidelity' claims; a more standard comparison (e.g., against real captured footage or perceptual studies) would strengthen the photorealism argument.

The 'dynamic score' comparison (Fig. 6) against real monocular datasets (Nerfies, D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyCheck) mixes fundamentally different data sources (synthetic multi-object scenes vs. real single-subject video), making the comparison somewhat apples-to-oranges as a measure of 'motion diversity.'

Several baseline configurations required non-trivial manual fixes (e.g., reduced grid learning rate for 4DGS to avoid NaN losses, scene-specific solver parameter tuning), raising some concern about whether baseline comparisons are fully tuned/fair across all scenes.

The benchmark, while diverse in material type, has a modest total scene count (17) and relies on only 2–4 cameras per scene, which may limit statistical robustness of per-scene conclusions and multiview reconstruction quality assessment.

The paper contributes no new method to address the identified limitations of existing DyNVS approaches on physics-rich scenes; it is purely a benchmark/evaluation contribution, which is reasonable for a dataset paper but means the demonstrated 'significant potential for improvement' is left entirely for future work without any concrete proposed direction being validated.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified and important gap in Dynamic Novel View Synthesis: existing physics-aware benchmarks are largely limited to single objects/single materials, while PhysGaia offers 17 scenes with rich multi-body interactions across four material categories (liquid, gas, rheological substances, textiles), each simulated with material-appropriate solvers (FLIP, Pyro, Vellum, MPM).

Provides genuinely useful ground-truth information beyond RGB: 3D particle trajectories and physical parameters (viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, temperature), enabling quantitative evaluation of physical realism rather than only photorealism, which is a meaningful methodological contribution (TD and AUOP metrics).

Thorough empirical study: evaluates five recent DyNVS baselines (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, MoSca, SoM) under both monocular and multiview settings, across all 17 scenes, with both photorealism metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, FID/KID) and physical-consistency metrics, revealing a consistent and interesting finding that current SOTA methods achieve reasonable photometric quality yet fail to recover physically plausible motion (needle-like artifacts, trajectories that merely fluctuate near surfaces).

Good supplementary documentation: detailed description of solver choices and physical justification, per-scene physics parameters, camera trajectory setups, licensing information for all assets, and extensive per-scene quantitative/qualitative breakdowns, supporting reproducibility.
Demonstrates additional utility of the dataset for inverse-physics parameter estimation (PAC-NeRF, GIC), broadening the potential research use cases beyond reconstruction benchmarking alone.
Well-motivated comparison tables (Tables 1-3) clearly positioning the contribution relative to prior DyNVS and physics-simulated datasets.
weaknesses: The dataset is entirely synthetic (rendered via Houdini path tracing); no real-world captures are included, and while this is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, it leaves open how well conclusions transfer to real dynamic scenes with less idealized material behavior and sensor noise.

Physical realism evaluation (TD/AUOP) is only reported for two scenes (cow and box-smoke) in the main paper, rather than across the full 17-scene benchmark; this narrows the evidentiary base for the claim that existing methods broadly fail at physical realism, even though qualitative figures and the appendix partially support generality.
Inverse-physics parameter estimation is evaluated on only a single scene (bouncing balls) with two baselines, which is a fairly thin empirical demonstration of this claimed use case.

The correspondence procedure between reconstructed Gaussian primitives and ground-truth particles (matching j(i) at the initial frame) is not deeply analyzed for scenes with topology changes (e.g., splashing, fragmentation), where primitive counts and topology can diverge substantially from ground truth; more detail on robustness of this metric would strengthen confidence in TD/AUOP as evaluation tools.

Camera coverage is relatively limited (2 or 4 spiral cameras per scene), which, combined with the synthetic-only nature, may limit the diversity of viewing conditions relative to real handheld capture benchmarks the paper compares against.

The physics simulators rely on simplified constitutive models (e.g., Kelvin-Voigt viscoelasticity, incompressible flow assumption), so the 'ground truth' physical trajectories, while consistent with the chosen physical laws, are themselves approximations; this is mentioned but not deeply discussed in terms of how it may affect downstream use for physics reasoning evaluation.

Limited diagnostic analysis of why baseline methods fail (e.g., no ablations isolating whether failures stem from lack of collision modeling, deformation network capacity, or optimization instability), which would have made the empirical findings more actionable for follow-up work.
